findings.where: Draft additions to rule 2 ("What 'plainly shows' needs", tests (i) and (ii); last sentence on bodily reactions) and H89-FOLLOWS in rule 17, against guide v1.2 rule 15, which must stay as written.
findings.problem: Four places where the new text changes how rule 15 works without editing it. (1) Rule 2 now says "A clear pair needs one of these": tying words that say one thing brought the other, or a memory arriving with one of five speed words. Rule 15(a) lists "came to him" as words that show a direct bringing. "came to him" passes neither test, so the same words give a clear pair for a sign (rule 15a) and a held pair for a smell (rule 2, H89-FOLLOWS). The Part A sayings for ^9, "The thought came to me" and "It just popped into my head", fall the same way. (2) Test (ii) opens with "A memory, a picture or a thought of something else arriving at once" and its guard says "Test (ii) is about a memory or a picture arriving". The two sentences disagree on "thought". A thought that arrives "instantly" on a sign would be a clear pair by the first sentence. Rule 15 says "Speed proves nothing either way." That leaves a door to open question 1. (3) H89-FOLLOWS covers "A memory, a picture or a thought" that follows something noticed. A thought that follows a sign is also rule 15(d). One entry can carry only one certainty, so the teams can split between held and uncertain. (4) "A smile, a warmth or another bodily reaction is not a ^9 (rule 15)" is wider than rule 15, which says "A bodily reaction alone is not a ^9" and gives a flinch or a startle. A warmth is a feeling.

findings.problem: A dropped entry is in no row. So when one team's side of a disagreement is dropped, the miss costs one entry, not two, and E goes up with no change in labeling. Checks C7 (pointer labels) and C6 (a pair must point back) drop exactly the readings the teams disagree on. The 5% limit is on all of a team's entries, so one Noetic can lose a quarter of its entries while the verdict still counts as valid. This is a path to a false pass in ^8 and ^9, the two rows the draft expects near the bar.

findings.where: Measures section, "Pointing ceiling"; matching STEP 10 reasons FIELD and NAMING; Table 2 sum "pointing (FIELD + NAMING)"; the sentence "Perfect pointing alone would lift only ^8 and ^9 over 0.80."
findings.problem: The ceiling is too high, for three reasons. (1) It counts pointing misses per entry and takes the smaller team total, so two entries can lean on one partner. One-to-one pairing forbids that. (2) The sketch calls two ^4 or ^7 entries NAMING when their measures are in the same sentence; the written rule says the measures must overlap. (3) For ^2, ^3 and ^5, NAMING needs only the same Mind and one shared sentence. Many such pairs point at different things, and some turn on questions the draft itself lists for the owner. They are filed as pointing. No bar hangs on this line, but the owner will read it to tell a pointing problem from a meaning problem.
findings.evidence: merge_final/reasons2.py line 83 (smaller of the two team totals) and lines 49 to 50 (same sentence of the measures). Paired one to one by the written rule (mv_review/t9.py): ^9 has 16 pointing pairs, not 18, so the ceiling is (43+16)/(90-16) = 0.797, not 0.847, and it is under 0.80. ^6 0.673, not 0.705. ^7 0.486, not 0.514. Pairs filed as NAMING whose labels share no word at all: ^2 6 of 10, ^3 3 of 3, ^5 10 of 24, ^7 12 of 16 (t8.py, t9.py). Examples: V041 "shaped every gesture" against "Years of daily milking"; V291 "a client's address" against "the heavy toolbox"; V273 "the neatness of the new bottles" against "the fresh reagents". Without those pairs the ceilings are ^2 0.629 (draft 0.747), ^3 0.639 (0.724), ^5 0.563 (0.659), ^7 0.339 (0.514). For ^8 the no-shared-word pairs are real second mentions tied by the same Effect, and its ceiling stays 0.845.
findings.smallest_fix: Count pointing pairs one to one. Split NAMING in two: "same words, other start" (the labels share a word at the same place) and "same sentence, other label". For ^2, ^3, ^4, ^5 and ^7 only the first goes into the ceiling. Print the second as its own column and do not call it pointing. Make the sketch and the written rule say the same thing for ^4 and ^7.

findings.where: pointing_rule_exact_text, step 5 second bullet (a scene or a happening) and rule 6(e); matching step 5 (SAME_THING, start at most 2 words apart)
findings.problem: The rule does not fix where a happening label starts. It gives four lead-in examples ('She was', 'He saw', 'He had seen', 'he pictured'). It does not say what to do with the Mind's own name, with words like 'automatically' or 'would', or whether to label the action or the object of the action. Rule 6(e) allows both ('a thing the Mind meets' or 'something the Mind does'). The scorer forgives only 2 words at the front. So two rule-following labels of the same thing can miss.
findings.evidence: V291: 'Sam, an apprentice locksmith, automatically reached for the heavy toolbox.' Three labels the draft allows: 'automatically reached for the heavy toolbox' (next word after the Mind), 'reached for the heavy toolbox', 'the heavy toolbox' (the draft's own why-text for 6(e) names it this way). My run of the draft's test: first against third, start gap 3, no match. The middle one matches both. V158: 'Judge Davies would strike her gavel twice' against 'strike her gavel twice', gap 3, no match. V002: 'Tom arrived at the pool' against 'the pool', gap 3, no match. Owner's own cases: 'He had seen countless pallets' against the W2 label, gap 3; 'watching her grandfather shave' against the W1 label, gap 4. The draft's own numbers show the size: on the old labels ^5 is 0.447 with the start rule and 0.563 without it.
findings.smallest_fix: Add three sentences to step 5. (1) For something the Mind does: never include the Mind; start at the doing word; skip helper words (had, would, was) and -ly words in front of it. (2) For something another person or thing does: start at that doer's naming. (3) Never label only the object of the action. Then make the 6(e) examples follow it ('reached for the heavy toolbox', not 'the heavy toolbox').

findings.smallest_fix: Make the class mechanical. One sentence: 'In a passage where you write a ^9 with reached_by reasoning, every piece the Mind checks on the way to that conclusion is written as a clue (relative_to empty, clue true), even when it is also a feature of a named thing.' Keep the row split as it is.

findings.where: pointing_rule_exact_text, step 10, relative_to for ^6 (the whole)
findings.problem: The draft says the whole is 'found by nearness, which needs no judgment'. It does need judgment. The rule says 'the nearest naming of the thing the parts belong to' and 'skip count-or-group phrases'. Both halves ask what the parts belong to. Nearness and belonging give different answers on real passages, and one of them breaks an agreement the old teams already had.
findings.evidence: V131: 'Quinn learned how to service a complex derailleur. The task involved dismantling the main pivot bolt, the spring mechanism, and the cage assembly.' Nearness gives 'The task' (same form as the draft's 'The problem' in V199). Belonging gives 'a complex derailleur'. Both old teams wrote 'a complex derailleur' for these three parts. L1 against L2 under the draft scorer: 5 parts, 0 matched, all on the whole. V159: 'the steps for propagating her prize orchid' (both old teams) against 'propagating her prize orchid' (skip the group word 'the steps'): start gap 3, no match. V210: 'The opponent's strength' against 'his opponent's game': no match. Each such split costs every part in the list (4 or 5 entries per passage).
findings.smallest_fix: Add two lines and two worked examples to step 10. (1) 'the steps for X', 'the parts of X': the whole is X, starting at X. (2) Say which answer you want when the nearest naming is the work done on a thing ('The task involved dismantling a, b, c'), and show it. Then measure whole agreement on the practice pass before the freeze.

findings.where: presence_rule_changes, rule 6(b), 6(c), rule 17 H5-ROLE; worked example W2
findings.problem: Three gaps for ^5. (1) 6(c) says write a ^5 twin 'when one statement gives both'. It gives no test for that. W2 writes a clear ^5 on bare exposure ('countless pallets move down the conveyor belt'), while the question list says 'Is exposure alone ^5' is not decided. (2) 6(b) says a named habit counts ('a habit', 'ingrained'). 6(c) says label the experience and keep the forming words in the support. One sentence often holds both. (3) H5-ROLE lists 'the cobbler' and 'as a student', so every bare job title is a held entry.
findings.evidence: (1) Old labels: team A put a ^5 on the same words as its own clear ^7 in 0 of 66 entries; team B in 25 of 96. V291: L2 writes the twin, L1 does not: 1 extra ^5. (2) V398 'a familiar pattern ingrained by many isolated winters': L1 labels 'a familiar pattern', L2 'many isolated winters', no match. V285 'worked in this canteen for thirty-five years, seeing generations pass through': L1 'worked in this canteen', L2 'generations pass through', no match. Over the 12 passages: ^5 4 / 4 / 1 matched. (3) 80 of the 428 old passages open with 'Name, a/an/the role,'. Team A wrote a ^5 on that phrase in 14, team B in 21. A literal labeler now holds all 80.
findings.smallest_fix: (1) Take the twin away from the labelers. Let the program print ^5 with and without a program-made twin for each clear ^7. The owner's answer can then be applied with no relabeling. (2) One tie-break: 'If the sentence names an experience and a habit, label the experience. If the experience is only a length of time, label the habit.' (3) Say in H5-ROLE whether a plain job title with no experience word ('a taxi driver') is held or left out.

findings.where: presence_rule_changes, rule 6(a) rate test, rule 6(d), rule 17 'Order for ^7', worked example W2
findings.problem: The rate test is a word list. It lets in far more than the old teams ever marked, and three edges are not settled. (a) 'always', 'often', 'countless', 'whenever' pass, and the order paragraph says: if words pass, write clear or H7-NOEFFECT. (b) 'He had seen countless X over his N years' passes (ii), and W2 marks that same form clear ^7 plus ^5. (c) The line in (iii) between a plural thing and an activity is not stated as a test, and one example is misquoted. (d) The order paragraph reads as one pass per passage; H7-RESULT says 'the passage ... gives no words that pass'. It is not said whether the test is per passage or per thing.
findings.evidence: (a) 95 of 428 old passages hold a listed rate word. Both teams marked ^7 in 39, one team in 11, neither in 45 (K1 17, K2 13, K3 10). Examples: V248 'always made her wince slightly', V190 'This specific smell always brought back', V388 'he always smiled at her'. (b) V375, V225, V359, V369, V133: neither team marked ^7. V375 even states the effect ('now the damage only presented a familiar challenge'), so 6(d) makes it clear. (c) The draft lists 'decades of busy lunchtimes' as passing; V404 says 'Decades spent managing busy lunchtimes'. V428 'years of loading and unloading': both old teams marked ^7; the new test fails it. V398 'many isolated winters': L1 says a length of time (held, H7-RESULT), L2 says a count of repeats (clear). Result: 1 bar-row entry against 0. (d) V255: L1 writes H7-UNBROKEN and H7-RESULT, L2 stops at H7-UNBROKEN.
findings.smallest_fix: Add four lines. (1) 'Rate words count only when they say how often this Mind meets or does the thing. Rate words on what someone else did, or inside a remembered scene, give no entry.' Then say plainly whether 'always made her wince' is H7-NOEFFECT or nothing, with one example. (2) '(iii) passes only when a plural noun follows of. An -ing word after of or spent does not pass.' Fix the V404 example. (3) Say whether 'many winters' is a count or a length of time. (4) 'Apply the order to each thing, not once per passage.'

findings.where: presence_rule_changes, rule 10 (a), (c), (d), (f), (g); pointing_rule_exact_text step 9
findings.problem: Rule 10 contradicts itself once and is silent on four common forms. (1) 10(d) says 'comforting' is what kind, not how much. 10(g) uses 'once overwhelming, now ... a comforting hum' as its example of two sizes. (2) 'left him cold' is in 10(a) as a clear ^4 and in H3-NOPULL. 'held little appeal' is only in H3-NOPULL. It is not said whether it is also a ^4 measure. (3) 10(f) covers a how-much word on a pull or an aversion only. Not on comfort, anxiety or awe. (4) 10(c) says how a thing strikes other people is 'not ^4 for this Mind'. It does not say whether to write it for those others. (5) Step 9 says copy the shortest stretch; 10(g) says use the first statement.
findings.evidence: (1) V285: L1 follows 10(g), two entries. L2 follows 10(d), one entry. 1 matched, 1 extra. (2) Six old passages hold a no-pull phrase. Team A wrote ^4 on it in 5 of 6, team B in 2 of 6. V189 'held no appeal' and 'an undeniable pull': L1 writes two ^4 entries, L2 none. (3) V060 'a jarring intrusion': L2 calls it a size (the draft's own scorer note calls it one of 'two different sizes'), L1 calls it a kind under 10(d). 1 extra. (5) V255 'had become a quiet backdrop to her thoughts, unnoticed for years': L1 measure 'unnoticed', L2 'a quiet backdrop to her thoughts'. Same thing, same Mind, measures do not overlap: 0 matched. Five old sentences have this two-part form. Over the 12 passages: ^4 10 / 7 / 5 matched.
findings.smallest_fix: One line each. (1) Change the 10(g) example to one with a how-much word on both sides, or say that the 'now' half gets no entry. (2) State in 10(a) whether the H3-NOPULL phrases are ^4 measures. (3) Say whether a how-much word on any named feeling about the thing gives a ^4, or only on a pull or an aversion. (4) Say 'write no entry for unnamed others'. (5) 'If one sentence states the same size in two places, copy the first.'

findings.where: pointing_rule_exact_text, steps 2, 5, 7 and 11; matching step 5 (labels compared by position)
findings.problem: Three pairs of sentences point opposite ways on which naming to take. (a) Step 5: 'A name of the form X of Y starts at X.' Step 7: label the thing, not its quality. (b) Step 2: take the naming in the evidence sentence and do not swap it for an earlier one. Step 5: 'Never one bare word when the passage gives more.' (c) Step 11: use the first statement of the role. Step 7 gives 'He enjoyed restoring such items' as its example, which is the second statement in V181, and its thing is named two sentences back, not 'the same sentence or the one before'. Because labels are compared by position, picking a different sentence is a miss even when both labelers write the same words.
findings.evidence: (a) V134 'The rough texture of the tweed': both old teams wrote it whole. Step 7 read plainly gives 'the tweed': start gap 4, no match. Same for 'the intense heat of the quarry sun' (V047, both old teams whole, gap 4), 'the neatness of the new bottles' (V273, gap 3), 'The glint of the new, unused lock mechanisms' (V132, gap 3). (b) V184: the push is at 'recoiled slightly from the roses'. Step 2 gives 'the roses'. 'Never one bare word' gives 'the deep red roses' from the sentence before. The old teams split exactly this way. No match. (c) V181: L1 'an old, scuffed pair of leather boots' (step 7). L2 'the task' (first statement: 'knew the task would be a pleasure'; 'the task' is not on the pointer list). No match. V134: 'the tweed' in sentence 1 against 'the tweed' in sentence 4: same words, no match. Over the 12 passages: ^2 4 / 4 / 2 matched.
findings.smallest_fix: (a) Add to step 7: 'This step is only for a phrase that points at the thing with its, their, such, or the plus a bare noun. When quality and thing are in one X of Y phrase, start at X.' (b) Reword to: 'Never cut a naming phrase down to its bare noun. A plain re-naming that the passage itself writes (the mess, the roses) is allowed.' (c) Replace the V181 phrase in step 7 with an example that fits step 11, and say what counts as the first statement for ^2 and ^3: the first sentence with a word of affinity, pull or aversion aimed at the thing.

findings.where: pointing_rule_exact_text, steps 2 and 3 (going back from a pointer; no_fuller_name); checker C7
findings.problem: When the naming next to the evidence is a pointer, the rule says go back and 'take the first naming there that is not a pointer'. It does not say whether a describing phrase after 'was' or after a comma is a naming, or what to do when the sentence opens with some other noun. And no_fuller_name is the labeler's own call; the checker lets it through. The draft said its rule avoids judging that two phrases are one thing. In every pointer case that judgment is back.
findings.evidence: V008: 'Zach listened to the low, steady hum emanating from the hive. The sound was constant, a soft, vibrating drone. It suddenly brought to his thoughts a lullaby ...' L1 follows the letter: 'The sound' is a pointer, the next naming in that sentence is 'a soft, vibrating drone'. L2 says that is a description after a comma and goes back to 'the low, steady hum'. Result: ^8 0 matched, ^9 0 matched (the ^9 labels agree but their triggers do not). V077 and V277: the sentence before 'It brought to his thoughts' opens with 'The air'; the letter of the rule gives 'The air', gap 4 from the scent. V115 ^2: 'A quiet yearning for those simpler days'. L1 writes 'those simpler days' with no_fuller_name. L2 goes back to 'late-night study sessions'. No match.
findings.smallest_fix: Add to step 2: 'A describing phrase after was or after a comma is not a naming. Go back to the nearest sentence that names, with its own noun, what the pointer points at.' Add to step 3: 'Use no_fuller_name only when no noun anywhere in the passage names the thing.' Add V008 (as a made-up twin) to the worked examples.

findings.where: presence_rule_changes, rule 2 added paragraphs; rule 17 H89-FOLLOWS; checker C6
findings.problem: Four holes around pairs. (1) Test (ii) says a memory that arrives with 'suddenly' is a clear pair. The next paragraph says a second pair needs its own tying words. A second memory with 'suddenly' and no tying words falls between them. It is not H89 either, because H89 needs no sudden word. (2) H89 says 'just before'. It is not said whether one sentence in between is allowed. (3) The word list in (ii) reads as closed. (4) C6 needs each ^8 and its ^9 to point at each other. No rule says how to write several signs that lead to one conclusion.
findings.evidence: (1) V115 'She suddenly remembered the worn leather armchair' and V107 'She suddenly thought of the quiet library': team B wrote a second pair in both, team A in neither. L1 against L2 on V115: 1 extra ^8 and 1 extra ^9. (2) V072: a general sentence stands between the patient's wince and 'Samuel remembered his own childhood fear'. L1 holds the pair, L2 writes a note and no pair. (3) V116 ('She remembered her grandmother's linen cupboard', no tying word) and V192 ('a memory ... flooded his thoughts'): both old teams wrote a clear pair. The new tests move both to held, or split the teams. (4) Old labels: team A has 13 ^8 entries with no ^9 that points back, in 11 passages (7 of them K6). Team A (V126, V050) and team B (V191) both reported this gap.
findings.smallest_fix: (1) One sentence: 'A further memory with a sudden word but no tying words gets no pair.' (or the opposite; pick one). (2) 'Just before means the sentence before; one sentence of general remark in between is / is not allowed.' (3) Say the lists are examples and add 'flooded', 'came to'. (4) 'Several signs, one conclusion: write one ^8 for the first sign and one ^9; name the other signs in the support.' or allow one ^9 per sign. Pick one and show it.

findings.where: passage_plan, order of work step 2 (practice pass on 48 fresh passages)
findings.problem: The practice pass is the only place where these rules meet new passages before the seal. It is too small to show the splits above, and it has no pass mark. 48 passages over 11 kinds is about 4 per kind. It is described as a test of 'the entry format, the checker and the re-ask loop', not of the pointing rule. After the seal no rule may change, and a new attempt needs new passages.
findings.evidence: Each item above came from reading 12 passages twice. A practice pass with about 4 K1, 6 K5 and 2 K7 passages cannot show whether both teams take the naming in the evidence sentence, where they start a happening label, or how they sort clues. The bar leaves little room: with E = matched / (matched + only A + only B), a role both teams wrote but pointed at differently counts once on top and twice below. E of 0.80 needs fewer than 1 in 9 such roles to miss.
findings.smallest_fix: Make the practice pass about 120 fresh passages, weighted to K1, K2a, K2b, K4, K5 and K7 (15 to 20 each). Run the frozen-candidate scorer on it and print Tables 1 and 2. Write down before it runs what must be true to seal (for example: no rule conflict reported, and K1 pairs at or above the bar). If not, fix the guide and practice again on new passages. Practice passages are never scored for the verdict, so this breaks no conduct rule.

findings.where: expected_effect_and_what_will_still_fail (my forecast, as asked)
findings.problem: Which Noetics I expect to still fail under the proposed bar (E at least 0.80), and why. This is an estimate from reading, not a measurement. ^4 Vibration: FAIL. Presence is still open-ended; rule 10 contradicts itself on kind against size; 'held little appeal', 'undeniable', 'jarring' and how things strike other people are unsettled. ^7 Rhythm: FAIL or NOT_ENOUGH_CASES. The rate test has soft edges, 'effect stated' is a new judgment, action labels start in different places, and 45 of 428 old passages hold a listed rate word that neither team marked. ^5 Female: FAIL. Experience or trait as the label, the twin with ^7, named skill against skilled action, and team B marks more. ^6 Male: FAIL unless the clue line is made mechanical; the whole is still a judgment and one split costs 4 or 5 entries. ^2 Positive: under the bar. Thing, quality or use; first or later statement; the comfort hold line. ^3 Negative: under the bar or NOT_ENOUGH_CASES. A bodily reaction with no feeling named, and fear, have no rule; the two holds shrink the row. ^8 and ^9: about even, leaning under. The K1 pointing rule works on most passages I walked, but a pair fails if either end is off, second memories add extras, and fewer than 1 pair in 9 may miss. ^1 Mind: likely pass, not by much; side people are still unruled (team B 43 extra, team A 16).
findings.evidence: My 12-passage double labeling (hard cases): ^4 10/7/5, ^7 2/3/1, ^5 4/4/1, ^6 5/8/0, ^2 4/4/2, ^3 3/2/2, ^8 2/3/1, ^9 2/3/1, ^1 13/12/12. The draft's own measured ceilings on the old labels, if every pointing miss had matched: ^4 0.489, ^7 0.514, ^5 0.659, ^6 0.705, ^3 0.724, ^2 0.747, ^8 0.845, ^9 0.847, ^1 0.868. My reading agrees with the draft's summary except that I put ^8 and ^9 slightly lower and ^6 lower, for the reasons in the items above.
findings.smallest_fix: Put this forecast in front of the owner beside the bar question, so the number is chosen knowingly. Fix the one-line items above before the practice pass. Do not add rules for ^4 and ^7 presence beyond those lines; the open points there are the owner's to answer.
